name: sealed-case-class
intent: Fix the alternative shapes of a domain value in the type system: a sealed base type declares the complete, closed set of cases and one immutable data type carries each case's own fields, so invalid combinations cannot be built and every case analysis can be checked for completeness.
problem: A domain value really comes in a small, fixed set of shapes - a payment is a card payment or a bank transfer, a request is pending, served or failed - but the code models it as an open class hierarchy with nullable fields, a tag plus a generic payload struct, or a bare enum with side tables. Nothing states that the set is complete, so a forgotten alternative surfaces as a runtime failure (a null dereference, an unhandled switch arm, a MatchError), and a new case silently changes behaviour instead of breaking the build. The pattern is the decision to close the variant set (`sealed`) and give every case its own immutable data type (`case class`).
context: Data-centric domain modelling where the alternatives are decided by the domain rather than by third-party extension: result and status types, domain events and commands, small state machines, ASTs, and payloads exchanged inside one service. It presupposes a declaration the compiler or an external checker can see in full (sealed/permits/enum/union alias) and a team that accepts the closure contract: adding a case becomes a deliberate, compiler-guided, source-breaking edit that must never cross a published extension boundary without an explicit unknown / `non_exhaustive` escape.
benefits: The complete set of alternatives lives in one declaration, so the type - not a comment or a runbook - is the source of truth for that part of the domain vocabulary.

Case analysis can be checked for totality: a forgotten alternative is a compile error (Rust, Swift, Java 21, Kotlin `when`-as-expression) or a promotable warning / type-checker error (Scala, C#, Python, TypeScript), instead of a runtime null, MatchError or silently skipped branch.
Each case carries exactly its own fields, so the invalid combinations a tag-plus-nullable-fields record permits (a card payment with an IBAN, a failure without a message) are unrepresentable.
Adding a case becomes a guided refactor: the compiler names every match that must be revisited, which is the strongest checklist available for evolving a vocabulary.
Case carriers are values: structural equality, `toString`, non-destructive copying and decomposition come for free, so tests, logs and caches treat them as data rather than as objects.
Immutability makes cases safe to share across threads, cache and replay: an update produces a new case value instead of mutating a shared one.
tradeoffs: Closure is a breaking-change contract: every added case source-breaks every non-exhaustive consumer. That is intended inside one codebase and unacceptable across a published extension point or a third-party implementation - those need an explicit escape hatch (`#[non_exhaustive]`, an `Unknown` case, a tolerant wire reader).

Expression-problem skew: cases are cheap to add and operations are expensive (a new operation touches every case and every match). An open hierarchy with virtual dispatch has exactly the inverse cost profile, so the choice should follow the axis that actually churns.

The guarantee is only as strong as the toolchain: a hard error in Rust/Swift/Java 21, a warning in Scala (and in Kotlin/C# outside expression position), a type-checker or linter feature in Python/TypeScript/Go, a build flag in C, and absent in Ruby and plain JavaScript. Review cannot substitute for the missing check, and the record must not promise more than the language delivers.

Immutability is shallow by default: `final`/`val`/record/`frozen` protects the binding or the field slot, not the object behind it, so a mutable collection field quietly reopens the illegal states and breaks equality and hashing.

Ergonomic and layout costs: the cases must be declared where the base is (Scala same-file, Kotlin same-package/module, Java same module), `null`/absent is not a case, and updates allocate (`copy`/`with`), which is fine for domain values but visible in hot inner loops.

Fat bases are tempting: sharing fields or behaviour on the sealed type erodes both halves - the sum degenerates into a tag plus a record, and the shared behaviour attracts operations that should have stayed per-case.

participants.responsibility: Declares the closed universe of alternatives - `sealed trait`, sealed interface/class, `enum`, abstract record, or a discriminated-union alias - and is the type consumers match on; the compiler uses it to know the complete set.
Immutable carrier of exactly one shape (`case class` / `data class` / record / enum variant / frozen dataclass); holds only that case's fields and never mutates.

The sanctioned way to build a value (companion `apply`, `new`, enum variant, factory or smart constructor); sets discriminant and payload together, so an inconsistent tag/payload pair cannot be created.

Case analysis whose branches correspond one-to-one with the cases - `match`, `when`, pattern `switch`, `std::visit`, visitor - written total and without a catch-all arm, so the compiler can detect a newly added case.
Converts untrusted or wire data into the closed type once (validating the tag, rejecting or explicitly naming unknown variants) so interior code only ever handles complete values.

use_cases: Outcome types such as `Ok`/`Err`, `Loading`/`Loaded`/`Failed` or `Parsed`/`Rejected` shared across a domain layer or driving UI state.
Domain events and commands with a vocabulary that is fixed for one bounded context (`PaymentCaptured`, `PaymentRefunded`, `PaymentDisputed`), where each event carries different fields.

Recursive structures - expression trees, document models, protocol frames - with one case per node kind eliminated by a single recursive match (using `indirect`/`Box`/sealed cases for the recursive case).
Payment instruments, shipping options or similar models where each alternative has its own fields and a nullable-field struct would permit nonsense combinations.
Option-like types (`Present[T]`/`Absent`, `Some`/`None`) that the compiler forces every consumer to handle.
State machines whose states carry their own data (connecting, open with a session, closing with a reason), so transitions become matches over closed sets.
Jetpack Compose's Android offline-first architecture models `AuthorUiState` as a sealed interface with `Loading`, `Success` and `Error`, so a UI can render every repository outcome explicitly.

The JDK's `java.lang.constant.ConstantDesc` sealed interface closes the family of nominal constant descriptors (`ClassDesc`, `MethodHandleDesc`, `MethodTypeDesc` and constant wrappers) used by bytecode tooling.
Rust's compiler AST (`rustc_ast::ast`) uses enums such as `ItemKind` and `VariantData` to represent syntax alternatives, keeping parser and compiler matches explicit.
Scala 3's `Option` ADT (`Some`/`None`) demonstrates the same closed, parameterized-versus-singleton case split using enum syntax.

Swift's standard library `Result` enum fixes the outcome vocabulary at exactly two cases, `.success(Success)` and `.failure(Failure)`, each with its own associated value, so every consumer `switch` must handle both arms.

Akka Typed persistent actors model an event-sourced entity's `Command`, `Event` and `State` as sealed traits with concrete case classes (`Add`/`Added`, `Clear`/`Cleared`, `EmptyAccount`/`OpenedAccount`/`ClosedAccount`), so command and event handlers are total matches over the persisted vocabulary.
avoid_when: The set is genuinely open - plugin points, framework callbacks, user-implementable interfaces: use an interface or abstract class with documented extension points (Strategy, Adapter) or the Extensible Visitor pattern; sealing a published API turns every new case into a breaking change.

The payload must survive across service or schema versions where unknown variants are normal: use a tolerant wire format with explicit unknown handling (Protobuf `oneof`/`Any`, JSON with an unknown branch, `#[non_exhaustive]`) instead of binding the local type to a closed set.
The alternatives carry no per-case data: a plain enum or type-safe enum is simpler and sufficient.
The fields are independent rather than alternatives: the model is a product type (record/struct) - forcing a sum over an AND is a modelling error.

The behaviour is the stable part while the case set grows release after release (codec formats in a hot loop, for example): an open hierarchy with polymorphism keeps each operation's implementation local.
It is scaffolding inside one function: a tuple, a dict or two booleans are enough; the ceremony of a closed type is not paid back.
anti_patterns: Sealed base plus mutable case payloads (`var` fields, dataclasses without `frozen=True`, records holding live collections): the immutability half is dropped, so an "immutable sum type" changes under its consumers and sabotages hashing and caching.
A catch-all arm (`case _ =>`, `else`, `default:`) added to silence the compiler: it disables the exhaustiveness check and hides exactly the new-case sites the pattern exists to find.
Fat sealed base: hoisting shared or nullable fields onto the base so the sum degenerates into a tag plus a record again - illegal states return, and base behaviour now blocks per-case operations.

Using the base as a marker for "some domain object" (`sealed trait Entity`) and grouping unrelated cases into one match: the set is closed but meaningless, and consumers must handle alternatives they do not care about.
Chained `instanceof`/`isinstance` guards ending in `throw new IllegalStateException("unhandled")` in a language (or codebase) that could have verified totality statically.

Sealing an API you ship and then adding cases in minor releases: consumers' exhaustive matches or serialized data break in a patch, because the closure was a compatibility claim the project could not keep.
design_principles: Make illegal states unrepresentable: encode alternatives in the type instead of validating tag/payload consistency at runtime.
Totality over defensiveness: when the type system can prove all cases are handled, defensive `null`/`default` code only hides regressions.
Immutable value semantics: cases are values (structural equality, no identity, no mutation), hence freely shareable, comparable and testable.
Closed by design: the vocabulary is fixed where the domain says it is fixed; extension is an explicit decision rather than an accident of inheritance.
Single source of truth: one declaration names every alternative, and every consumer's completeness is measured against it.
best_practices: Keep the sealed base empty of state and behaviour; put fields and any case-specific behaviour on the cases.
Make the closure transitive: where `sealed` is not inherited (Scala cases, Kotlin indirect subclasses), mark every case `final`/`sealed`/`data` so nobody can reopen the hierarchy below the base.
Keep cases immutable: `val`/`final`/`readonly` fields, frozen dataclasses, records, and immutable collections (or defensive copies) for anything a caller could otherwise mutate.
Never write a catch-all arm in a case analysis over the closed type; if a case must be ignored, name it and handle it explicitly.
Parse, don't validate, at the boundary: convert untrusted data into the closed type once - rejecting or explicitly modelling unknown variants - so interior code sees only complete values.
Add cases with the compiler: declare the new case, then follow every newly reported non-exhaustive match; that refactor path is the payoff the pattern buys.
Keep operations as standalone functions/matches over the type rather than as methods on the base, so new operations stay visible and the case set stays independent of behaviour.

Tour of Scala, "Pattern Matching" - sealed traits, case classes, and the same-file extension rule; https://docs.scala-lang.org/tour/pattern-matching.html

Noel Welsh, "Everything You Ever Wanted to Know About Sealed Traits in Scala" (Underscore, 2015) - exhaustiveness checking, why `sealed` is not transitive, and why the static type of the scrutinee decides; https://underscore.io/blog/posts/2015/06/02/everything-about-sealed.html
Baeldung on Scala, "Algebraic Data Types in Scala" and "Sealed Keyword in Scala" - product/sum composition, sealed as the ADT closure; https://www.baeldung.com/scala/algebraic-data-types
Wikipedia, "Algebraic data type" and "Tagged union" - the sum-of-products concept behind closed variants and compiler-verified case coverage; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_data_type
Kotlin documentation, "Sealed classes and interfaces" - direct subclasses restricted to the same package/module and exhaustive `when`; https://kotlinlang.org/docs/sealed-classes.html

OpenJDK JEP 409 (Sealed Classes) and JEP 441 (Pattern Matching for switch) - permits-based type coverage and the MatchException contract when a hierarchy outgrows a compiled switch; https://openjdk.org/jeps/409

Scala 2.13 Language Specification, "Classes and Objects" - sealed classes are confined to one source file and case classes synthesize pattern-matching/value operations; https://www.scala-lang.org/files/archive/spec/2.13/05-classes-and-objects.html
Scala 3 Reference, "Algebraic Data Types" - enum cases model parameterized and singleton variants; https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/enums/adts.html

Android Developers, "Build an offline-first app" - `AuthorUiState` uses a sealed interface for Loading/Success/Error state in a StateFlow; https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture/data-layer/offline-first

Rust nightly compiler API, "rustc_ast::ast" - compiler AST alternatives such as ItemKind and VariantData are represented as enums; https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nightly-rustc/rustc_ast/ast/index.html

Java SE 17 API, "ConstantDesc" - the JDK sealed interface for nominal constant descriptors and its permitted descriptor family; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/constant/ConstantDesc.html
OpenJDK code review, "Summary and Recommendations" - critique of sealed types' practical exhaustiveness and API-evolution tradeoffs; https://cr.openjdk.org/~cushon/amalloy/sealed-types-report.html

Apple Developer Documentation, "Result" - the Swift standard library enum with `success`/`failure` cases carrying associated values, consumed by exhaustive `switch`; https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/result

Akka core documentation, "Event Sourcing" (typed persistence) - the canonical `EventSourcedBehavior` example defines `Command`, `Event` and `State` as sealed traits with case-class implementations handled by total command/event handlers; https://doc.akka.io/libraries/akka-core/current/typed/persistence.html

The Rust Programming Language, "Using Box<T> to Point to Data on the Heap" - why a recursive enum variant needs indirection (`Box<List>`) to have a known compile-time size; https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-01-box.html

Java Object Serialization Specification, "Object Input Classes" - enum constants are read back by name via `Enum.valueOf`, never by declaration ordinal, so ordinal-based tags desynchronize when cases are inserted; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/serialization/input.html
